### Explore relationship, between studied hours vs scored in Exam

```{r cars}

cor(dfm$hours_studied, dfm$exam_score)
```
#### Explore correlation matrix for all numeric predictors

```{r cars}
# Correlation matrix for all numeric predictors
cor(dfm[, c("hours_studied", "sleep_hours",
           "attendance_pct", "exam_score")])
```

###  Simple linear regression model(one predictor)
```{r cars}
# Model: exam_score = b0 + b1 * hours_studied + error
model1 <- lm(exam_score ~ hours_studied, data = dfm)

summary(model1)   # coefficients, R-squared, F-test, p-values
coef(model1)      # just the intercept and slope
confint(model1)   # 95% confidence intervals for coefficients

# Draw the fitted line on the scatter plot
plot(dfm$hours_studied, dfm$exam_score,
     main = "Simple linear regression",
     xlab = "Hours studied", ylab = "Exam score",
     pch = 19, col = "steelblue")
abline(model1, col = "red", lwd = 2)

```
##### prediction

```{r cars}
new_students <- data.frame(hours_studied = c(2, 5, 8))

# Predicted mean score, with a 95% prediction interval
predict(model1, newdata = new_students, interval = "prediction")
```
#### CHECK THE ASSUMPTIONS (residual diagnostics) 

```{r cars}
#  ASSUMPTIONS (residual diagnostics)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))   # 2x2 grid of plots
plot(model1)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))   # reset

# 1) Residuals vs Fitted : random cloud around 0 -> linearity OK
# 2) Normal Q-Q          : points on the line     -> normal errors
# 3) Scale-Location      : flat band              -> constant variance
# 4) Residuals vs Leverage: no point beyond Cook's distance lines

shapiro.test(residuals(model1))   # p > 0.05 -> residuals look normal

```

### MULTIPLE LINEAR REGRESSION (several predictors)

```{r cars}
#MULTIPLE LINEAR REGRESSION (several predictors) -----------
# Model: exam_score = b0 + b1*hours + b2*sleep + b3*attendance
model2 <- lm(exam_score ~ hours_studied + sleep_hours + attendance_pct,
             data = dfm)

summary(model2)
confint(model2)

# Compare the two models
anova(model1, model2)   # does adding predictors improve the fit?
AIC(model1, model2)     # lower is better
BIC(model1, model2)     # lower is better
```

### TRAIN / TEST SPLIT: HOW WELL DOES IT PREDICT NEW DATA?

```{r cars}

set.seed(123)
train_idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(dfm)), size = 0.8 * nrow(dfm))
train <- dfm[train_idx, ]
test  <- dfm[-train_idx, ]

model_train <- lm(exam_score ~ hours_studied + sleep_hours + attendance_pct,
                  data = train)
pred <- predict(model_train, newdata = test)

rmse <- sqrt(mean((test$exam_score - pred)^2))   # typical error size
mae  <- mean(abs(test$exam_score - pred))
r2_test <- 1 - sum((test$exam_score - pred)^2) /
               sum((test$exam_score - mean(test$exam_score))^2)

cat("Test RMSE:", round(rmse, 2), "\n")
cat("Test MAE :", round(mae, 2), "\n")
cat("Test R2  :", round(r2_test, 3), "\n")

# Actual vs predicted: points should sit near the diagonal
plot(test$exam_score, pred,
     xlab = "Actual", ylab = "Predicted",
     main = "Actual vs predicted (test set)", pch = 19, col = "steelblue")
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)

```
